data.title: OS Command Injection
data.summary: User input reached an operating-system command without being separated from the command syntax, allowing arbitrary commands to run under the account the application runs as. This is the shortest route from a web request to control of the host.
data.description:
Command injection arises when an application builds a command line as a string and hands it to a shell. Shell metacharacters in the input — `;`, `|`, `&&`, backticks, `$()` — are then interpreted as syntax, and the attacker's command runs alongside the intended one.

Features that shell out are a small and predictable set: file conversion, archive handling, imaging, network diagnostics, backup and reporting jobs. Any of them with a filename or hostname from the request is a candidate.

The result is code execution as the service account, which is the start of the real compromise rather than its end: credentials in the environment and configuration files, access to internal networks, and whatever the account's privileges allow on the host.
data.recommendation:
* Avoid invoking a shell. Use APIs that take the program and its arguments as an array, so no parsing of metacharacters takes place.
* Prefer a library that performs the task in-process over calling an external binary.
* Where a value must reach a command, validate it against a strict allow-list — not a blocklist of dangerous characters.
* Run the service as an unprivileged account, with the filesystem and network access it needs and no more.
data.short_recommendation: Call binaries through argument arrays, never through a shell.
